title: Don Smedley and Tom Stagg Interview, 1969-10-03

blocks.x: Tom Stagg of London, England, 3rd October 1969. Talking about jazz in England from the earliest recollection, I have is about 1949, at that time there were probably only two or three jazz bands, mainly based on the early dance bands of the period. The dance bands of that period were Billy Cotton and Harry Roy. The Savoy Havana Band and the Savoy Ophians, which played at the Savoy Hotel in London for a long period for many years, from the late 1920s, the British jazz bands originated from this type of music, probably partly due to the fact of the visit of the original Dixieland jazz band in 1919, where of course they used a British pianist, Billy Jones. Now the first recollection of a band I have, George Webb's Dixielanders, they played at a place called the Red Barn in Bexley Heath, Kent, which now is an outer London suburb, at that time was a separate Kent town. I can't recollect the personnel right now, but they played King Oliver numbers, and ODJB numbers, they were a very tightly arranged band, stuck mainly to the original scores and were pretty popular. They had, I can remember Bob D'Orban on trombone, who is now on the staff of the Melody Maker newspaper, writing on pop music, but at that time was a very good traditional style trombonist. This was the same time that Ken Collier became interested in, a little later, probably about 1950, 1951, Ken Collier came on the scene with a friend of his Sonny Morris. Sonny Morris still leads small bands of his own, but at that time the two played together in Middlesex, which again is now an outer London suburb, but at that time was a separate town. Now they played improvised jazz completely, there was much more earthy and ethnic folk music, they stuck nothing at all to any set arrangements or scores. They were playing, it's hard to say the tunes right now, they were playing tunes they'd heard on record, but not sticking to the, they were all 78s of King Oliver and Armstrong around at that time, they were sticking to these tunes, but they weren't sticking to the arrangements, they were just playing, this was the first improvised jazz in England. And they cut a few records for a small private label of their own, and then eventually on a label called, uh, A Squire, which was run by a fellow called Carlo Cramer, who is still active in England on the record producing side. The first jazz concerts I attended were probably around this time, about 1952, 53, after Ken Collier had left for New Orleans. The Mike Daniels band from Croydon, the Croydon area where I lived and always have lived, were around at that time, they were playing at the Croydon Jazz Club, a fellow by the name of Frank Getgood, who promoted in the Croydon area way back then, and still does today, he's one of the biggest promoters and enthusiasts in the South London area. And they used to, uh, to, uh, hold, uh, concerts at a place called the Civic Hall in Croydon, which is now pulled down, there's a, there's a big store in its place. And the Mike Daniels band used to play, the very early Humphrey Littleton band used to play there. And the Humphrey Littleton, the first Humphrey Littleton band I saw, uh, was made up of members of the Melody Maker, Paul Winners, award concert. At that time Eric Delaney, the drummer Eric Delaney, is now of course a showman, and a swing drummer, he's got his own little band, and he's on tour for, what, 52 weeks of the year, playing in holiday camps and ballrooms throughout the country. Humphrey Littleton at that time had, had a purely traditional style band of trumpet, trombone, clarinet, and drums, bass, and guitar he was using at that time. They were playing, uh, again, uh, mainly Armstrong and Oliver numbers, but Littleton must have been one of the first jazz musicians in England to write his own numbers and to arrange his own numbers, and these things are gradually, sort of, infiltrating into the British music scene. This is probably about 1953. Littleton also was one of the first, um, jazz bands to get a major recording contract with Parlophone records, and recorded extensively with Parlophone on 78s for, must have been ten years or so, probably as much as a, one issue a month at that time. And so he was the most well-known band at the time. The smaller bands around, the Ian Bell band, played at, uh, a place called the Park Lane Ballroom in Croydon, which was next door to the Fire Station. All been pulled down now. Uh, the Red River Jazz Band were around at that time. I can't remember the personnel. These were local bands. But mainly the Humphrey Littleton band at that time. There was also the Chris Barber band came into existence around that time. Uh, Collie was still away in New Orleans. Chris Barber had a small band of his own, mainly playing in the London area. They played at the Hammersmith's Palais for an Aspire record concert. Uh, Barber again was playing, he was playing sort of semi-arranged jazz even at that time, but putting in a few numbers of his own, probably following along the lines of the Humphrey Littleton band at that time. It was only very small, there's minority musicians, there were probably about, no more than about 30 around in the London area at that time. There's one very...
May I interrupt? Would you come from... come from, uh... the, uh... perhaps... 1949, the, uh, Ken Collier, the Queen River? You come from there. Yeah.

Ken Collier came back from New Orleans in, in, in late 1953, and this altered really the whole aspect of traditional jazz in England. The first thing he did was to, to get together the finest of the traditional musicians of that time in the country, and, um, he chose Chris Barber on his rumbum. Before that, for a very short period, a fellow called Ed MacDonald, who came from the north of England. He used Chris Barber and Dizz Disley on guitar, and banjo at that time. And these were the finest musicians of, of that period. This was about 1954. Uh, he came back with a whole range of new ideas and new tunes. He'd been out here for some time. You know, he's generally known, and he cut some records out here with, I mean, he'll Barnes. And this changed the aspect entirely, because after a few months, a lot of small bands were cropping up everywhere, playing a sort of Ken Collier style jazz. And even today, there are Ken Collier inspired trumpet players. About the same time, the Humphrey Littleton band went its own sweet way, still playing semi-arranged stuff. And Littleton was a great man for, for experimenting, and, uh, he ended up with a, what he called his, his, his, his, his, his, his, his, he ended up with a, what he called his, his Pazio band, by adding, um, uh, sort of African bongo players, and I was giving him a sort of West Indian teach. So he went one way, the, the, the, I think Collier band went the other. Well after a few months there was trouble in the Collier band between Collier and Chris Barbara, and they decided to split up and go their own separate ways. Collier, um, chose a, and, well what happened was that technically Barbara sacked Barber sacked Collier, Barber keeping the remainder of the band, and Collier choosing different musicians. From that day onwards, of course, Chris Barber has never looked back. He now plays, he no longer plays in the traditional idiom as such, but ranges on Duke Ellington and even modern rhythm and blues tinges, and plays mainly on the continent now where the work is. Collier has stuck to his early principles and still plays basically the same music as he did when he started, and he's stuck to more or less a steady personality. He's had very few personnel changes. He was recording for Columbia Records for some time, and then his contract expired with them, and he's no longer got any sort of recording contract at all now, and he records on a variety of small independent labels, so he still has quite a steady output. Chris Barber does a tremendous amount of promoting as well, and our jazz and blues festivals, we've had about eight now for the past eight years, are promoted partly by Chris Barber. You can see how his music has changed by the types of bands and musicians he's had at these jazz festivals over the years. The early ones were purely traditional style music, and one of them included Lewis Nelson with the Barry Martin Band, and today this, the 1969 jazz festival was purely rhythm and blues and soul time music, which is now what Barber is playing, with basically the same personnel, although he adds an electric guitar, a fellow by the name of John Slaughter, who played electric guitar. These two main bands, the Littleton and Barber, and the Ken Collier Band, the three bands in fact, were the three main bands through the late 1950s. About 1958-59, there were many small amateur bands, people playing, young fellas just playing for the fun of it, were springing up all over the place. One in particular, the Barry Martin Band, started about 1959, and that time using Keith Smith on trumpet. They played mainly in their own little area in Surrey, for small dances and scouts.
Now may I ask you, from where is Barry Martin spring?

Barry Martin spring? He's a sort of hometown boy from a place called Virginia Water. His father's family comes from a musical family. His mother sang at one time. His father, I believe, played saxophone, or he played drums or saxophone in his small dance bands for many years, and he went into the green grocery business. Barry had heard these bands of Littleton and Barber and Collier, and was duly inspired. And from about the age of fourteen, he was knocking about on drums then. He had a few local fellas around, and they used to play about a three piece band for Boy Scout dances, and our British Legion dances. He held up with Keith Smith at that time, and they were very friendly at that time. And their first little band was known as the Frondzy Me Band, was in 1958. Well, not a very popular band, but a very local band in the Surrey countryside. They used to play small jobs, carnivals and things like this. Well, late 1959, Barry had sorted out what he wanted to do and what he was going to do. Keith Smith had gone his own separate way. And Barry then had a regular band, and they had their first London job in about 1959, the Studio 51, the Ken Collier Club. And they got the residency every Wednesday. They had a Wednesday night residency there. And that was their first London job. And they never really looked back from there. Barry went about seven years without a personnel change in his band, except for the trumpet player, who never did take it very seriously and decided to retire at an early age. What was that? What was that? Clive Blackmore, who was a Kid Howard-inspired trumpet player, but he was only ever an amateur, and he was quite satisfied in the early days of doing these local jobs. But when Barry decided to broaden his outlook, then Clive went his own way, and Cuff Billet from Portsmouth joined the band. And that band stayed together for about seven years. Now, in 1961, Barry decided it was about time he found out more about it, and to come to New Orleans. He had no money at all, though I can recollect a little story. I was with Barry the night before he left for New Orleans in 19 February 1961. They were playing a job at a place called the Palm Court in Pearlie, which is now again a London suburb. It wasn't then. And Barry had exactly thirty shillings in his pocket and was due to leave for New Orleans the following morning. And he went to New Orleans via Canada and he worked in a boot factory in Canada, putting laces and shoes, and eventually this type of work. He worked in a road gang and all this type of thing. And eventually, after about eight months, arrived in New Orleans with about a thousand dollars, he'd say. While he was here, he made two recordings. At that time, he wanted a dance band sound. He recorded Kitchig Swingsters, which was a regular band at that period. And he also recorded Kid Hats.

Howard was John Handy. It's interesting in this respect because John Handy had never been heard of in England before 1961, and of course Handy's gone on to great things since then. This is partly due to Barry's efforts in England and on the continent. He came back in late 1961, early 62, duly inspired a far better drummer. He had lessons from Joe Watkins and Si Frazier, and this had changed his outlook completely. He kept the same personnel but took them off the road, and they did very few jobs while he sort of knocked them into shape with what he wanted them to do. And this is the difference. At that time, by this time it was about 1962. The Chris Barber Band had gone on to being a very professional unit. The Ken Collier Band had stayed exactly as it was, and it still is. The Humphrey Littleton Band had gone on to a more progressive style. And people at the Barry Martin Band, the smaller bands, were beginning to become known. This was just before what was known as our trad period in England. There were many, many small bands cropping up at that time. The Barry Martin Band was just about the finest of the bands around at that time. There were literally hundreds of small bands cropping up overnight all over the country, including Ackerbilt, really, which came up from the west of England. And the Terry Lightfoot Band, which were very well known in England. There were a lot of bands at this time. Well, Barry knocked his band into shape, and he decided the only way, the thing to do for the fellas in New Orleans was to start promoting as well. He played through 1962, working on a first tour. And with the help of Sammy Remington, who is well known in America, and in Europe for that matter now, he now resides in Denmark, Sammy. He has a band in Denmark. They decided to bring over Kid Sheik. It was a very amateur effort that I helped on this very first tour. We had no idea that we had to have Ministry of Labour permits, work permits, etc. What happened was, we just wrote to Sheik and asked him if he would come, and he said yes. He jumped on the boat, arrived at Liverpool, and they promptly decided to send him back. Because he had no work permit, nothing at all. A frantic phone call from the Board of Trade, in rushing about, and they decided to let him stay, providing he took it as a holiday. And he didn't work here. Well, eventually, Kid Sheik stayed here in England for about three months. He played about four nights a week with the Barry Martin Band. Another band, he played with Keith Smith, and any other band he could get work with. And he was quite happy with this arrangement. And he was the pioneer, Kid Sheik was the pioneer of real New Orleans music in England. He taught the local fellas a hell of a lot. And also promoted the Barry Martin Band. Before this, the only other band that had come to England, a New Orleans band, was in late 1959, when the George Lewis band came over. George Lewis himself came over in 1957, and played with the King Collier band. It wasn't a great success. It wasn't widely advertised, while it wasn't widely publicised. But for the few who saw George with the King Collier band, this inspired many people. The person promoting Paddy McKeeran lost a tremendous amount of money over this early tour. But Harold Davidson, who was about the largest promoter in England, decided in 1959 to have a sort of three band project. He brought over the George Lewis band, the Kid Ory band, and Earl Hines. They lost a tremendous amount of money. The whole project was shelved. And this was another one of the reasons why Barry decided that these things were done on a smaller scale. They could still be done. And after the sheep tour, it was decided between a sort of small society we set up, a small group of people in the south of England, a small group in the north of England, to try to bring over at least one or two musicians from New Orleans per year. This helped in many ways. It gave the New Orleans musicians more work, and they became widely known, especially people like John Handy. But it also promoted the Barry Martin band tremendously. Kid Cheek went back on. He was followed the following year, 1964, by Kid Thomas and Emmanuel Paul. And at the same time, late in 1964, George Lewis came to play with the Barry Martin band. It was the second to last tour of George May. The Martin band still had the same personnel, the same type of music, and still are today, for that matter. By 1964, 1965, the British sort of trad period had just about petered out. British music된 stuff된 된 stuff된 stuff된 stuff된 stuff 된 stuff 된 stuff 된 stuff ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! stuff You have the trad period, the sort of country and western period, the folk period, and then the sort of pop, rock and roll, soul period. It'll all go around again in one big circle. It's pretty quiet on the traditional side at the moment, you see, since about 1964. From that time, the 6th of 1964, the bands that were left, Ken Collier has gone his own sweet way, still plays on pretty quietly, doing the same things he always has done. Humphrey Littleton now plays only progressive jazz. He has a line-up of trumpet and about three saxophones, baritone, horn, melton and soprano on occasions, and plays mainly progressive jazz for private parties. He was playing one job a week at the Six Bells at Chelsea, and they have visiting musicians, the type of Jimmy Witherspoon, and this type of singer does work with the Humphrey Littleton band. Chris Barber and Ken and Ackerbill mainly stay on the continent now. They do most of their work in Germany, and even as far as Poland, behind the own curtain. Of the smaller bands, Barry Martin band is still going strong, and the small bands such as John Casimir's band and the brass band side... Mike Casimir, who has a band and also leads the only brass band we have in England, in the Midlands, there's Dan Pawson's band, and other small ones which are quite well known to a minority, well known in their own particular area. If anything special happens, they all group together, and are known by the chosen few in England that follow this type of music. As far as recordings go in England, the smaller bands don't really get a chance. No major recording company will entertain a small British jazz band at all these days. Barry Martin records mainly for Doug Doble's 77 label, and a subsidiary label called Swift, and of course for his own labels, he runs Mono and Rhythm Records. Steve Lane's band mainly, or only record really, for their own VJM label. And this is the set up. There isn't a major company in England which will record British jazz, well not even the progressive style. Columbia, now and again, will record a modern band, but the traditional style musicians, they don't get a looking unless they they record for their own labels, or for a label which is only closely connected with local traditional music. That's really about like the whole set up with British jazz as such, other than the brass band period, which started, again, the first brass band to play was around about 1960. Kichik played in a brass band in 1961 in England. He was the first New Orleans musician to play in a brass band in England. I believe to this day is the only one to march with a British brass band. Mike Casimir is the only organised brass band at present. They're playing for carnivals, fates, and what we have as donkey derbies, and this type of thing. Very spasmodic work. They're mainly pick-up bands, they're not steady personnels at all. They play only really during the summer. They do protest marches, and C&B banner bomb marches, and this type of thing.
Would you explain that donkey derbies?

The donkey derbies? Well, the donkey derbies sort of originated in rural England, way back now, probably in the late 1880s, where they have a group of donkeys, and usually children are jockeys, and they name all these donkeys, and they name their races. They're like a small horse race, and they run only about 20 yards, and only a few shillings on each one. In fact, there's one held every year in a place called Wallington in England, and one of the races is named the Paragon Stakes, after Mike Casimir's Paragon Brass Band. It's like Morris dancing in England. It's part of sort of English heritage, rural English heritage. And really, that's the brass band's saying. Anything else?

My... I first became interested in traditional style jazz while I was still at school. I was born in 1938. This was in about 1948, 49. The first record I ever bought was Louis Armstrong's Basin Street Blues, which I bought second hand at some ridiculous price of about eight shillings at that time, was a hell of a lot of money. I was doing a paper round and had seen this record in a post office, and had saved for about four weeks to buy this record, and hoping it hadn't gone. I used to go down and look at this record for about four weeks before I could afford to buy it. I bought this record and it was overjoyed. This was the very first record I'd ever heard. This was, as I say, by Louis Armstrong. I went on from there, decided I would buy some of this music on record. And I bought a few Humphrey Littleton 78s, and eventually, I think it was for a birthday or part of a birthday present, I bought one of the first LPs by the Humphrey Littleton band. I can recall it was called Humphrey the Conway, and the Conway Hall was a hall in Red Lion Square, London, where they used to hold early Humphrey Littleton band concerts. At that time, I went further and went on and on and bought every record I could afford to buy by every band imaginable. This was before I decided to specialise in just New Orleans music. There was no New Orleans music as such then. They were all bands such as the Armstrong 78s and the British bands. We'd only heard of George Lewis and Bunk Johnson in those days. There were no records about them, although very, very few and far between. The first jazz concert I went to was at the Civic Hall in Croydon, and I saw the Ian Bell Band and the Red River Band. The Ian Bell Band were an offshoot of the George Webb Dixielanders. I only ever saw George Webb's Dixielanders once in person. It was about the same time, just before they broke up. It must have been about 1950, 51, just before the band finished. Most of the musicians joined either the Ian Bell Band or some other small bands around at that time. These concerts were held once a month in Croydon, and I don't think I missed one between 1950 and about 1954. Still collecting records all the time. About 1955 I had such a tremendous collection of odd records that I decided to specialise in just New Orleans music. Excluding the long-term expatriates like Armstrong and Kid Orry, mainly for the reason at that time, and it still applies today, is that through lack of money there was so much music about of one sort that to specialise you had to cut out the other types of jazz, which I still have to today. Not because of any dislike, but the preference is and always has been. I can remember going down to a local record store in Croydon, England, and taking all these great heap of 78s and a few LPs down there of the British stuff and selling them or part exchanging them for what all the music I could get. And I did this through about 1955 to 1957. Now in 1957 a few people... ... ... ... ... ... ...

Graham Russell and a girl, Ray Whittrick, decided to form a Bunk Johnson Appreciation Society, and they were holding once a month meetings in a pub, the Porcupine, just off Charing Cross Road in London. I joined this with my brother at that time, who was beginning to play a little bit of banjo, and we joined it, and the first meeting we ever went to must have been in late 1958, when Graham Russell came out of the Air Force. The first records we heard were the folkways Music of New Orleans, and it was in 1958 I first heard the Bunk Jazz Informations, and managed to buy a copy of the Commodore as well at that time, of the Jazz Informations sites. This did a tremendous amount of good. This society had a membership of perhaps 200 or so. The London meetings only had about all 10 or 12 people turn up once a month, but we used to take records and exchange records and buy records, and this was a basis of all our collections, I think, at that time. Barry Martin turned up at these meetings at that time. He was a keen record collector then. I think we all acquired our first American Musics at that time, probably beaten up 78s at that time. The first LP I ever, American Music LP I bought was at that time, I paid a fantastic price for it, about £4. It was the Bunk 44 American Music, and I've still got the original one to this day, and I've only ever played it about once. I have two copies of it, and I've never played this original one more than about once or twice. It was a new one as well, and I was so proud of this. It was a new one as well, and I was so proud of this. These meetings, we had trouble at this pub we were using. We had to move to another pub, and gradually, less and less people came to these meetings petered out. But the Bunk Society still produced a newsletter and sold records, and we had our own record label at that time, known as Purist Records, which we had a sort of Bunk reissue programme. We had a couple of unused American Music sites issued on it, and some Bunk with Doc Evans we issued. We were very proud of these things, and mainly sold them only to members. There were about 5, 78s and 2 LPs issued over a period of about four years. This got me interested in record production and also a little bit of writing at that time. I used to write for one or two very short articles for a couple of magazines around at that time. One published in the Midlands in Birmingham by a guy called Les Page. And I did a little bit of writing for this small magazine. In about 1956 the Bunk-Johnson Society folded through lack of support. And things were pretty quiet from... around that time for a couple of years, and mainly stuck together. The people from the Society, we corresponded and exchanged records and news. George Lewis had turned up early in 1957, and we'd seen our first New Orleans musician. I can remember the Stoll Theatre in Kingsway in London, which has now been pulled down, all standing outside in the crowd, gazing in awe at George Lewis, who was the first New Orleans musician ever to come to this country. And he played some concerts with the King Collier Band. In late 1958, early 59, when the George Lewis Band turned up, George came with Kid Howard and Jim Robinson, Slowdrag, Joe Robichaud and Joe Watkins. We all turned out at Euston Station in London to see the band arrive. And this was our first real encounter with New Orleans musicians. We spoke to them and we had parties and we got to know them all personally. And this was a great thing. Before that time we only had such a few records in comparison with today, and there were only really names on record labels and on sleeves. We didn't know any of them personally. And we got to know them all personally. And we had some marvellous times. And I in particular travelled most of England following this band around. I saw about eight concerts out of the twelve. I think it was twelve they did, and I managed to get to about eight of them. Well that band went back, and they went out onto the continent and eventually went back. And I then, by this time I knew Barry Martin pretty well, because I'd met him through this Bunk Johnson Society, which had now folded. In early 1963 I decided to write to Ray Whittrick, who had been running this society, and asked what had happened about it. She still had the mailing list, one thing or another, but it was doing nothing. It was pretty stagnant. And she said, well if you want to take over the running of this society, by all means do so. I've still got all the mailing lists and all the people interested. The record side was defunct. So I took over the whole of the set-up of the Bunk Johnson Society, and for a couple of months produced a monthly newsletter. Decided it was pretty useless to carry on calling it the Bunk Johnson Society, because nothing was happening as far as Bunk Johnson was concerned. We were generally dealing with New Orleans music, so I changed it to the New Orleans Jazz Appreciation Society. And this society exists to this day, although it's pretty quiet and doesn't do a lot, but it keeps two, three hundred people informed of what's going on through letter, word of mouth, telephone calls, etc. etc. in England. In 1963, as was mentioned earlier, Kichik arrived, and it was decided that the only way to do this properly was to form another society. This is an idea of Barry Martins, to deal mainly with promoting New Orleans musicians in England, at that time only England. And the Promotional Society for New Orleans Music was formed. The first musicians to come over with this society was Kid Thomas and Emmanuel Paul. And they came to England in 1964. After this tour, a northern promoter became interested in this. He could see that there was something in England for this type of music, and decided that he would bring over George Lewis with this society of ours to tour with the Barry Martins band. And George Lewis came, I think, now, if I remember correctly, it was September 1964. And had an extensive tour and a recording session. And this 1964 tour was probably the foreignist tour that George Lewis made in England and the continent. Only in England was the Barry Martins band, but it was a very, very good tour. George was playing very well at that time in England. And this was probably the finest tour George made in England. In late 1964, Alton Purnell came, not promoted by the Promotional Society at all, but by Keith Smith. Keith Smith became interested in promoting, and entirely on his own, brought over Alton Purnell. In 1965, I officially became attached to the Promotional Society, and Don Smedley, sort of semi-officially became our official photographer, as he is now called. The first thing we all worked on together, that's the two of us and Barry Martins, was the Harold Dejan tour of 1965. And probably Harold had the most influence to the people in England. He was such a friendly guy, and mixed so well with the British public, and they accepted him so much. And although he turned up without a saxophone, and we had to hire him a horn, because we didn't dare bring him in. We were still avoiding board of trade and permits on one thing and another in those days. And he turned up just with his mouthpiece, which he told the customs people was his lucky charm. And we hired him a saxophone from some place in Wales. We had to go as far as Wales to find him a saxophone. And Don and I toured with Harold, well, all the jobs he played in England, which were down in Wales, a lot round the London area, and up to the north of England as well. He was so popular wherever he went. And Harold was the first musician in England to record with a brass band, and he called it the Young Olympia Brass Band, using only British musicians. The same day, he recorded a set of dance tunes, recorded live at a dance. This is the most peculiar dance, it was a works dance, and had people there ranging from 60 to about 16. And the impression we had was that this wouldn't go down at all well. None of the people there at all had heard of Harold Dejan or New Orleans music at all, but Harold turned up and completely took the place over in about five minutes flat. And it was quite an odd line-up as well, because Harold played alto, and we had Frank Brooker on tenor, John Coles on amplified guitar, Terry Knight on bass and Barry on drums, and it was a real little dance band sound. And from that day to this, that line-up hasn't been used in England at all. This is quite something. This was recorded at the time, live, and this was my first dabble in issuing records. I issued this particular recording with Barry Martin on a label which was known as New Orleans Anthology, which was a one and only effort because, again, we got into a bit of trouble with the performing rights society over it, and because we hadn't paid our dues on one thing and another. Although we paid for the session, we hadn't paid all the official things we had to be paid, so that was a one and only effort on that label. This was in 1965. In 19...we decided then that Harold being so popular and his first tour, discounting the George Lewis tour, which was promoted by an outside promoter, that these tours were going so well at that time, and the Barry Martin band in particular was very popular, that I joined...I became a partner in the promotional society, and I joined the Barry Martin organisation, became Barry's band manager, and also the one who looked after him on tour, looked after the band. We were on the road, did most of the driving on the road, and this was in late 65 and early 1966. The next tour we promoted in 1966 was again Kid Sheik, because he'd been pretty popular, and we brought over John Handy. This, again, was a very good tour. This was the first time that all his musicians had gone over to the continent, and Sheik and Handy went to Belgium, and this was the first time this had happened. They were very, very popular in Belgium, especially Handy. This was when Handy was becoming well-known outside his own country, and things were beginning to go well for him, you know, the other recordings, etc. This was a very good tour, it went well. It was followed, while Sheik and Handy were in England, Keith Smith, through a German promoter, Lippmann and Raal, decided to bring a band to Europe. And Alvin Elkhorn came with Jimmy Archie, Donnell Howard, Elton Pennell again, Saif Frazier and Pops Foster. This was the last tour that Donnell Howard was to make, of course. He died shortly after, and not long after, Jimmy Archie. While they were here working for Keith Smith in England, Keith Smith covered the English side of this tour for the German promoters. Sheik and Handy still being here, we had quite an epic recording session, known as the Eagle Brass Band. We recorded inside, using Sheik and Alvin Elkhorn, and Keith Smith on trumpets, Saif Frazier on bass drum, and Barry Martin on snares, Handy on alto, and the rest was made up of local musicians. Jim Young on tuba, who later recorded with the Olympia Brass Band. This was recorded for George Buck, who to this day hasn't issued this session yet, but it's a very, very fine session, and quite a historic session, as far as English recordings go. And this brings us up to 1967, when we worked on a tour and brought Lewis Nelson to England. Now, Nelson had a very good tour of England, and also went to Belgium. We tied up with some Italian people, who were not promoters, but just enthusiasts. They'd heard a couple of New Orleans records, and when I say a couple, this is literally true. Between a gang of a...

about six or eight of them, they had about five records between them. And they had written and asked me, in fact, if they could have Chic and Handy, but they'd left it so late it was impossible to organise anything with Chic and Handy, but we said the next musician we bring to England, we would offer them. We offered them Lewis Nelson, and they jumped at the idea. So we flew with Nelson to Milan. Now Lewis Nelson was the first New Orleans musician ever to go to Italy. And it has worked out today that he's paved the way for every subsequent musician that comes to England now takes in Italy as well. So Nelson paved the way. He was a tremendous success in Italy, and they wanted him to stay longer, although being under contract with us he couldn't. We played in Milan, in Genoa, smaller places, Sandrio for the finish of an Italian professional cycle race, I remember. And we played, these cyclists all arrived, and they gave out the trophies, and we played the session afterwards. And Nelson was so popular, although none of us spoke Italian, and very few of these Italians spoke English. We sort of communicated through the music, and were treated so well, it was really something quite fantastic. They looked after us in the best hotels, and we only worked about, we were there in Italy about ten days, and we only did about five jobs in ten days, and they looked after us all the time. We went down to Genoa to do a job in a club in Genoa, the Louisiana Jazz Club in Genoa, which is in a little courtyard, rather like a New Orleans patio, rather of the soul of a court of two sisters in fact. And this little club is a fantastic club, they've got all posters, stuck all round the walls, and they've got various trophies, which they give to themselves. They've got their own little band, the Louisiana Jazz Band, who play only about once every two months. They have a session, and they've got this whole jazz club there, and no one ever comes, and they just play for themselves. And now, of course, they've got all the photographs of the Nelson tour, and probably, Nelson was the only person I went to Italy with, but they've probably got photographs of the other musicians there as well now. And this place was packed solid for about two nights, and this is the only time this has ever happened there. And we had a really fantastic time. This was, as I say, in 1966. When we came back to England, George Lewis was waiting for us. We had a second tour with George Lewis, and this was rather a sad occasion for us, really, because this was the last tour that George ever made. Before Nelson was due to return home to the States, before he went, the day before he went, we did a recording with the Barry Martin rhythm section, which was Graham Patterson on piano, Barry on drums, and Brian Turnock on bass, Cuff Billet on trumpet, George Lewis on clarinet, and Lewis Nelson on trombone. This was the only recording at that time which Nelson made in England, and turned out to be the last record George ever made. I think I'm right in saying that that's the last recording George Lewis ever made. The tour went well at the beginning. We travelled the length and breadth of this country, taken in places like Nottingham and Manchester and Birmingham. And in fact, George Lewis played one job in Birmingham with the Ken Collier band, and was the only other time between 1957 and 1966. That's the only New Orleans musician that Ken Collier had played with, between all that time. And this was the only other band that George played with on that tour. Now towards the end of the tour, that George Lewis tour, we were in the north of England. We played in Rotherham and Manchester. And we came back to London, that's the Barry Martin band. We came back to London and left George in Manchester, because of course he had his manager, manageress with him, Dorothy Tate, and she insisted on so many hours and so many days rest in between the jobs. So we decided to leave him in Manchester in the hotel. The Manchester Sports Guild, who were promoting this tour, and who had promoted the earlier tour of George Lewis with the Barry Martin band, decided and asked Dorothy Tate if George would play another job with a local band, a local Manchester-based band. As George was feeling pretty fit, and he hadn't had any illness at all while he'd been in Europe. He'd been taken to having his nasal spray and his tablets and things. And they asked Dorothy Tate if George would play one night with this local band. And if I remember correctly, Dorothy said, yes, this would be OK, providing George only played two sets of 45 minutes in the evening, with a gap in between. Well, George played the first set. This was on a Thursday night. In fact, we only had one other job to do with George. The Barry Martin band had only one other job in Nottingham to do on the Friday. Well, this was on the Thursday. We were all down in... back in London. And George played the first set with this local band and collapsed during the second set. I had a frantic telephone call. I was in bed about 7 o'clock on the Friday morning, and I had a frantic telephone call from Dorothy Tate to say George had collapsed on the stand, had been rushed into a hospital, a private room, in a hospital in Eccles, which was a suburb of Manchester. She was beside herself, really didn't know what to do. So I said, well, you stay exactly where you are, and I'll come up immediately. This is about 7 o'clock in the morning, on the Friday morning. I phoned Barry Martin and told him, well, you'd better cancel the job at Nottingham and tell them that we couldn't do this job because George had been taken as sick at that time, not knowing what was wrong with him. And I rushed up to Manchester by train to see Dorothy Tate. I met her in the hotel, and she was really in a bad way. She was beside herself, didn't know what to do, what to say or anything. I said, well, the only thing we can do is go out and see George and see how he is. At that time, she hadn't seen George. They'd taken him to hospital. So we went over to this hospital in Eccles, which is way out of Manchester, and saw George in this private room. He really did look sick. I'd only seen him about two days previously to this, and he was so full of life and had felt better than he said. He'd felt better than he had for months. And he was laid on the bed, naked on the top of the bed, and he looked so ill and drawn. He'd knock the stuffing clean out of him. One extra job would just sort of click. But of course, knowing George as we knew him, he said there was nothing wrong with him, and he'd be out of bed in about two days. He was fussing, and because Dorothy Tate was making such a fuss over him, he was getting annoyed, and seemed quite happy in his own way. And I sorted out what had to be done as far as each other's jobs were concerned, and that, of course, our contract had been broken, and that nothing would come of this, and I tied up the loose ends with the Manchester Sports Guild and came back to London. Of course, we had no work then. Our jobs... We had this one other job which had been cancelled, so I said to Barry, we will take it easy for the rest of these couple of days, and I'll go back up to Manchester at the end of the following week, which I did. George was still in hospital when I went up there. He was much better walking about in the room, and Dorothy said she'd made arrangements for him to fly home. Just before he flew home to New York, from Manchester to New York, I left and I came back to... I said cheerio in Manchester to George. In fact, that was the last time I saw George. And I heard Dorothy phone me. I phoned Dorothy just before... She made the arrangements to go back through New York before coming back home. And just before they left, Dorothy phoned me to say George had been taken sick again, but the doctor decided he could travel. And they flew him to New York, and they put him into hospital in New York, and they put him in an iron lung for... It's a couple of days, I think. And he stopped on the way down to New Orleans again, and had treatment before he ever came home. And of course, that's the last tour George ever made, and that's the last time I ever saw George was in Manchester. It was very sad. Well, that was in 19... late 1966. Uh... 1967. 1967. Uh... The... The local music scene in England had died down. It was the... the tail end of our sort of trad period. There was not too much work about... The Barry Martin band had... had... had... had personnel troubles. The trumpet player decided that his day job was far more important than the music he was playing, and decided to quit. Barry then employed Dan Pawson for a little while, from Birmingham, a band leader from Birmingham. This was not a good union at all. Barry also worked with Keith Smith. The band... didn't work much at all. I finished my business with Barry, and we went our own separate ways, although even to today we're still very friendly, and we do work a little together on the recording side, with Don taking the photographs. Uh... Nelson was called back to Italy by these Italian people, and went straight from the States to Italy, made a very long second tour, which apparently didn't go too well, whether it was because he was by himself and felt a bit out of place, I don't know. But on his way back he pulled into England, and did a couple of... I think that's right, Don, he made a couple of private jobs while he was in England. I didn't personally catch him when he came back the second time, but he made a couple of records with Barry. One with... with Mike Casimir's Brass Band, although the record came out under Barry's name, but in fact it was Mike Casimir's Brass Band, for Lacroix Records, and this was... and the second one was just Lewis Nelson with Barry Martin's band, and this is the only recording of... uh... uh... the Barry Martin Band with Dan Pawson. They only played together for a very short period. Uh... Lacroix Records were just beginning then, and this was the first, um... we heard of Lord Richard Eakins as a record producer. Before then he was just an enthusiast from Birmingham. Uh... as I say, I went my own separate way. At that time I was doing a lot of writing. I wrote a lot of sleeve notes. I did sleeve notes for George Buck. I did sleeve notes for Pearl records. The stuff for Pearl to date hasn't been used, but some of the stuff for George Buck has been used. Uh... I was writing for Jazz Journal, Jazz Times, a local book, and a small magazine from Birmingham, which I can't recall the name of at the present, and generally doing a lot of historic... historical work for New Orleans music and for the musicians in England. In fact, I have my own little archives and a record collection, which consists of, um... almost every issues recording of New Orleans music, including all the Negro bands and also the mixed bands as well, which includes the bands on tour. in... in the States, in England, and on the continent. Very few recorded examples of New Orleans musicians on the continent at present. That took us up to 1967. In 1968, Kid Sheik had a... No, late in 1967, that's right, Kid Sheik shot through England on a... very quick visit. He was in England for about one week, and I think he did two jobs as well, didn't he, Don? I thought I remember... Yeah. ... when he came back, to work mainly in Belgium and Italy. While he was there, he made a recording. Uh... in... 1967, the same applied with... John Handy. He shot through England for about one week, taking in about two jobs with the Barry Martin band, on his way to... to... going to Belgium and Italy. Uh... Halfway through 1967, of course, the Olympia Brass Band turned up, and this was the first... New Orleans Brass Band we'd ever had in England at all. Tied in with the Southern Travel Directors Council, we had really nothing at all to do with it, except we tried to organise a party. We organised a private party for the... for the fellas while they were in England, but, um... officially, we had nothing to do with the promoting of it at all. Although, fortunately, um... the... uh... UK side of the Southern Travel Directors Council allowed us to partake in all the official business which they had to do at the Hilton Hotel, and also one job for the Salvation Army. They... they allowed... they allowed us to partake in all the... what was going on, which they had to do. They included us in it, which was very nice of them, because they had no... there's no reason why they should do it, but they included us in... in these things. It was a fantastic occasion for us. We went completely mad for a couple of days, taking photographs and... and, uh... as I say, this private party, which went down very well, this... halfway through 1967. Between then and 1968, nothing happened at all. It's a completely dead period. There was the ban... the ban work was... in England has been... has been... literally nothing. The ban's really scraped around, and... and... and... mainly playing in... in sort of pub jobs, where... where... it's something like... the Kitty Halls. The ban will play in a London... or a London suburb pub, just for... for what they can get by passing...

And this is really sad for England because to us we've gone down a stage. We got to a very good period where British traditional style bands were playing concerts. And big jobs, the Royal Festival Hall, the Conway Hall, which we've already mentioned. The Royal Festival Hall has symphony concerts and symphony orchestras. And the British traditional bands got to this stage where they were playing this type of job. And we now feel as if we've gone down a stage. That the English bands are now playing these pub jobs which are really few and far between. The Studio 51, the Ken Collier Club as it's known, was always open five nights a week. It was never opened on a Tuesday and a Thursday but it was open five nights a week. Doing two sessions on Sunday and an all-nighter from Saturday night to Sunday morning. They're no longer all-nighters. And just before we left to come to the States, the Studio 51 had a rhythm and blues band in there on Saturday night. And no traditional band there at all. Ken Collier plays there sometimes on a Saturday, sometimes on a Sunday. But it's pretty sad. The Barry Martin Band is about the only other traditional band to play there now. It's not open during the week at all. And this is the main, was the mecca of traditional jazz in London. The only other club running traditional style jazz is the 100 Club in Oxford Street. That is still open seven days a week but again is employing rhythm and blues bands and rock and soul bands and this type of music and private parties. Every now and again when the Kenny Ball or the Chris Barber Band or the Ackerbilt Band are back in England, they'll do one job at the 100 Club while they're in passing through. So it's come to this now. We've got plenty of London pubs having jazz bands in them, which are very nice for the public, but not too good for the musicians concerned. They're all virtually pick-up bands. There may be perhaps a dozen in the London area of these places going. So you can hear music for seven nights a week, which as I say is nice for the people but not too good for musicians. There are no small bands making a living out of traditional style jazz at the moment. The larger bands, people like Comfrey Littleton, only play when they're called for a job. It's not a regular band. They play society jobs a hell of a lot. And weddings or parties when they're called to play. The Kenny Ball, the Ackerbilt and the Chris Barber bands all play on the continent, mainly in Germany and Poland, majority of the year. The Ken Collier band has a steady amount of work around the country, but Ken Collier has his own devout followers, which he's always had, and can keep a steady amount of work going in this way. The jazz clubs are petering out as such. We had jazz clubs all over the country. We still have jazz clubs all over the country, but they're now farther apart and are more spasmodic, whereas they were once a week or once a fortnight. They're every other month now, this type of thing. Up to 1968, the last tour we had of a musician ourselves was Andrew Morgan, again only taking in one week in England, and again Italy and Belgium, this being of course that they're spending more time on the continent because the work is now on the continent. And sad but true, it isn't worth keeping an all-us musician. It cannot afford to keep an all-us musician in England when the Italian promoters are paying, and the Italian and Belgian promoters are paying most of the costs to bring them to Europe at all. The Olympia Brass Band came back again in September-October 1968, a larger unit this time, which was even better than the first, on their way to the Berlin Folk Festival. It stopped only two days, but managed a party and a recording. And from that to October 69, nothing has happened at all. It's been very, very quiet. The Baron Martin Band made an extensive tour of the United States, taking in the Orleans Jazz Festival. I myself have been keeping pretty quiet but active, dealing mainly with my own archives and files and recordings and letters and filing and keeping the music alive in England as much as possible. Up until now our visit here where we've been doing a lot of research and hearing a lot of music, meeting a lot of people, some great people we met, not just musicians, but just musicians. But other visitors in town, we've met a great lot of people, people like Eric Brown, who I only personally knew by letter. It was nice, and Yoshio, the Japanese trumpet player, it was nice to meet these guys who we only knew by letter and to meet in one place. And I've learnt a hell of a lot on this tour and I've got a tremendous amount of work to do now when I get back to add this to my own particular files to keep it going in England as much as possible. One good thing when we get back next week is that two days after we get back a manual sales arrives. So for a little while we'll have a bit of New Orleans back in England again for a short period. And that's just about the score. Another thing you say, Don? Nothing to write today. Nothing to write today.
